title: Terraform State Management
summary: What the state file is for, why hand-editing it is dangerous, and how a team shares it safely without stepping on each other.

slides.markdown:
Terraform's **state file** (`terraform.tfstate`, JSON) is its record of what it believes exists — every managed resource mapped to a real-world ID, plus last-known attribute values. Without it, Terraform can't know `aws_instance.web` corresponds to an already-running instance — it would try to create a new one instead of managing the existing one.

State is also how `plan` diffs cheaply: it compares code against **recorded** state first, refreshing from the real API only when needed.

Where the state file actually lives.

| | Local state | Remote backend (S3+lock table, Terraform Cloud) |
|---|---|---|
| Location | A file on one engineer's disk | Shared, centrally accessible storage |
| Team safety | Two people can silently clobber each other's changes | Locking prevents concurrent applies |
| Secrets exposure | Easy to accidentally commit to git | Access-controlled, not in git history |

Local state is fine solo; any team using Terraform for real infrastructure needs a remote backend from day one, not as a later migration.

Two engineers running `apply` at the same moment, against the same state, could each read a stale copy and write conflicting changes back — corrupting the state file. **Locking** prevents this: before an `apply` (or `plan`, in most backends) starts, Terraform acquires a lock (e.g. a row in a DynamoDB table alongside an S3 backend); a second apply attempted concurrently waits or fails until the lock is released.

This is why the classic S3 backend setup always pairs an S3 bucket (the state storage) with a DynamoDB table (the lock) — the bucket alone has no locking mechanism of its own.

![A team sharing state through a locked remote backend](assets/remote-state-locking.svg)

Every engineer's Terraform CLI reads and writes the **same** state through the backend, and the lock table ensures only one apply is ever in flight — the second engineer's apply simply waits its turn instead of racing the first.

assets.alt: A team sharing state through a locked remote backend

slides.markdown:
**`terraform import`** brings a resource that already exists — created by hand, before Terraform managed it — under management, by writing a matching entry into state. You still write the HCL resource block yourself, matching the real config; import only wires up the state-to-reality mapping.

Get the HCL wrong and the next `plan` shows Terraform wanting to "fix" every attribute you didn't match — a signal to double-check the block against the resource's actual settings.

`terraform state rm` removes a resource from state **without** destroying the real infrastructure — useful when you want Terraform to stop managing something (splitting it into a separate config) while leaving it running. `terraform state mv` renames or relocates an entry in state, matching a refactor in your HCL (e.g. moving a resource into a module) without Terraform thinking it needs to destroy and recreate it.

Both are last-resort tools for exactly this reason: they edit Terraform's understanding of reality directly, bypassing plan's normal diff-and-preview safety net.

slides.subTitle: Recovering from state out of sync
slides.markdown:
A `plan` shows Terraform wanting to recreate a resource that's actually fine — someone likely modified it outside Terraform. First, `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows what state thinks vs what the API reports, with no resource changes proposed. If state is just stale, `apply -refresh-only` updates state to match reality.

If state is missing the resource entirely, `terraform import` re-establishes the mapping — always safer than hand-editing the JSON state file, which risks corrupting entries you didn't intend to touch.

slides.subTitle: Committing local state to git
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "the state file is just metadata, fine to commit alongside the code."

**Why it breaks:** state files routinely contain **secrets in plaintext** — a database password, a generated API key, anything Terraform needed to configure a resource ends up recorded unencrypted, exactly as sent to the provider's API.

**The correct model:** state belongs in a remote backend with access control and encryption at rest, never in git — `.gitignore` should exclude `*.tfstate*` from day one, before anyone forgets.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: a stuck lock or corrupted state stops the whole team
slides.markdown:
State locking prevents concurrent applies, but it has a failure mode of its own: a CI job that crashes or gets killed mid-`apply` can leave the lock **held forever**, since nothing ever ran the release step. Every engineer's next plan or apply -- for any change, to any resource -- now blocks on a lock nobody is actually using. `terraform force-unlock` exists for exactly this, but it's a blunt instrument: force-unlocking while an apply is genuinely still in progress elsewhere is how state gets truly corrupted, not just locked.

A staff engineer's response to a stuck lock is to first confirm the lock-holder is actually dead (check the CI run, not just the lock's age) before force-unlocking, and to treat state file **corruption** as a restore-from-backup problem, not a hand-edit problem: a remote backend with versioning enabled (S3 versioning, Terraform Cloud's state history) means the fix is `terraform state pull` from a known-good prior version, not attempting to patch broken JSON by hand under incident pressure.
